title: Issues and Impediments
sequence: impediments and issues appear whenever work is done, from the first iteration or work package to closure. Manage Project Execution produces the issue log, Monitor and Control Project Performance uses it, and Close Project or Phase expects all issues resolved.

header.html: Business Environment domain (26%) · Task 4 Remove impediments and manage issues — evaluate the impact of impediments · prioritize and highlight impediments · determine and apply an intervention strategy to remove or minimize them · reassess continually so impediments, obstacles and blockers for the team are being addressed · recognize when a risk becomes an issue · collaborate with relevant stakeholders on an approach to resolve the issues

Topic 21 (risk register, risk responses, escalating risks) · Topic 24 (removing impediments during execution) · Topic 25 (supporting the team) · Topic 26 (conflict) · Topic 12 (escalation paths and thresholds) · Topic 29 (change requests that resolve issues) · Topic 28 (reporting issues) · Topic 04 (agile roles, daily meetings) · Topic 31 (retrospectives and lessons learned) · Topic 13 (collaborating with stakeholders) · Topic 35 (issues resolved before closure)

Glossary (impediment / blocker, issue, risk escalation) · Section 4 artifacts (issue log, change requests, risk register, lessons learned register) · Section 5 tools (daily coordination meeting, retrospectives, problem-solving, root cause analysis, cause-and-effect diagram, visual controls with an impediment list, prioritization/ranking, facilitation, decision-making) · Standard §2.4 and §2.5.2 (oversight, facilitation and support, sponsor and product owner decisions) · Governance domain (monitoring dependencies, risks, issues and escalations; §2.1.4 escalation) · Resources domain Lead the Team (resolving and escalating issues; servant-leader "support") · Risk domain (Implement Risk Responses, Monitor Risks, issue defined beside risk) · Close Project or Phase (all issues resolved)

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Impediment (blocker, obstacle) An obstacle that prevents the team from achieving its objectives. Examples: a waiting approval, missing access or data, a broken environment, an unavailable expert, a dependency on another group, an unclear decision
Issue A current condition or situation that may affect one or more objectives. It has already occurred or is occurring and may need immediate action or management attention
Risk An uncertain future event or condition (threat or opportunity) that has not yet occurred (Topic 21)
Issue log A project document in which information about issues is recorded and monitored
Impediment list A visual chart (one kind of visual control) showing each impediment's description, severity and the actions being taken to resolve it
Risk trigger An event or condition that indicates a risk is about to occur; recorded in the risk register
Problem-solving Finding solutions for issues or challenges: define the problem, identify the root cause, generate possible solutions, choose the best, implement it, verify that it worked
Root cause analysis Determining the basic underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk; a root cause may sit behind several of them, and when all root causes are removed the problem does not recur
Escalation Moving a matter to someone with more authority because it is beyond the team's or project manager's authority, or has persisted. For risks, risk escalation transfers ownership to a relevant party (Topic 21)
Change request A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline. When issues are found during the work, change requests are raised to correct them (Topic 29)
Dependency A relationship that makes one piece of work wait for another; internal and external dependencies are a frequent source of impediments, and governance monitors them together with risks, issues and escalations
Workaround Beyond PMBOK 8 A temporary response that keeps work moving while the cause remains; it does not remove the cause, so the item stays open until the real fix

2Risk, Issue, Impediment and Change Request: Telling Them Apart

Risk Issue Impediment Change request
Time Future, uncertain Present: occurred or occurring Present: blocking or slowing the team A proposal awaiting a decision
Recorded in Risk register Issue log Impediment list or board (and the issue log when it is also a project issue) Change log
Owner Risk owner Issue owner The person who can remove it, named Requester; decision by the authorized approver
Typical action Planned response; watch the triggers Analyze, decide, act; escalate if beyond authority Remove, work around or escalate Assess impact; approve, defer or reject
Exam wording "might", "could", "possible" "has now", "was announced", "is delayed" "blocked", "waiting for", "cannot proceed" "asks to modify", "baseline"

Key relationships

  • An issue can arise from a poorly managed risk; it can also appear with no risk behind it (an unforeseen event).
  • An impediment is an issue seen from the team's work: something that stops or slows the flow. The same loop applies to both.
  • A change request is one way to resolve an issue when a baseline or document must change (corrective action, preventive action, defect repair, update; Topic 29). It is not a synonym for an issue.
  • A conflict between people that disrupts the work is an issue to be resolved (Topic 26).
  • Beyond PMBOK 8 A false assumption, a missed dependency or a failed test can also create an issue.

3The Management Loop

Step ECO enabler covered Section
1 Capture and log Entry point for everything, including recognizing a risk that has become an issue 8, 11
2 Evaluate the impact Evaluate the impact of impediments 4
3 Prioritize and highlight Prioritize and highlight impediments 5
4 Choose and apply an intervention Determine and apply an intervention strategy; collaborate with stakeholders on resolving issues 6, 9, 10
5 Reassess continually Reassess continually so impediments, obstacles and blockers are being addressed 7
6 Close and learn Feeds the lessons learned register and OPAs (Topic 31) 11

Who does what

  • The team self-organizes and removes the impediments within its reach; it raises the rest at once (for example at the daily coordination meeting).
  • The project manager or scrum master (a servant leader) removes what the team cannot: works with outside groups, negotiates, re-plans, shields the team from outside disruption and escalates.
  • The sponsor, customer, product owner and governance bodies act on matters beyond the project management team's authority: decisions, funding, priorities, policy, and obstacles that sit in the wider organization (Standard §2.5.2).

4Evaluate the Impact of Impediments (ECO)

Understand before you act. Establish what is blocked, for whom, for how long and what happens if nothing changes.

Dimension Questions
Schedule Is the critical path, iteration goal, release or a milestone affected? How many days are lost for each day of delay?
Cost Idle time, rework, penalties, expediting
Scope and quality Which work is delayed, descoped or at risk of defects?
Resources How many people or teams are waiting? Is capacity or morale suffering?
Risk Does it raise existing risks or create new ones? Has a risk already occurred?
Stakeholders and benefits Which commitments, expectations or benefits are threatened?
Compliance and safety Is there regulatory, contractual, safety or ethical exposure?
Reach and control One team or several? Inside the team's control, or with another group or a vendor? Does it recur?

Find the cause, not only the symptom

  • PMBOK 8's problem-solving method: define the problem, identify the root cause, generate possible solutions, choose the best one, implement it, verify that it worked.
  • Tools: root cause analysis and the cause-and-effect (fishbone, Ishikawa) diagram. Beyond PMBOK 8 The "5 Whys" is a common way to drill down.
  • When several fixes have already failed, do not repeat the same repair and do not halt everything. Assess the impact and agree a different intervention strategy: work around it, replace the component, or reprioritize.

Record the evaluation in the issue log or on the impediment list so the priority and the strategy can be explained and defended.

5Prioritize and Highlight Impediments (ECO)

Prioritize

  • Rank open items by impact on the objectives and urgency, and work the highest first. Spreading the team across every open item resolves none of them.
  • Criteria: effect on the critical path or iteration goal; number of people blocked; cost of each day of delay (PMBOK 8 lists cost of delay among its prioritization methods, Beyond PMBOK 8 when used for impediments); downstream dependencies; compliance or safety exposure; whether the cause is inside the team's control; whether it recurs; how fast it can be removed (quick wins when impact is equal).
  • Beyond PMBOK 8 An impact and urgency grid is a common way to sort items: remove now, plan and own, quick fix or batch, watch.
  • Give every item one named owner and limit how many are worked at once.

Highlight

  • Keep an impediment list where the team and stakeholders can see it. PMBOK 8 describes this visual chart as showing the description, the severity and the actions being taken. It belongs with the other visual controls (information radiators), such as the task board, in a place people actually look.
  • Make it the first item at the daily coordination meeting and flag it on the task board.
  • Report upward: show key issues and the help needed in status reports and dashboards for the sponsor and governance (Topic 28), with the cost of delay in days or money.
  • Report honestly: no green status while the team is blocked (Topic 06).

6Determine and Apply an Intervention Strategy (ECO)

Strategy Use when Example
Remove the cause The cause is within the team's or project manager's control or influence Repair the broken environment; arrange the missing access; clarify the unclear decision
Work with the owning group The cause sits with another team, department or vendor, especially if it recurs Agree a standing approval slot or a service level with the central group
Negotiate or influence Resources or priorities compete Negotiate people's availability with functional managers
Re-plan or re-sequence The cause cannot be cleared soon Reorder the backlog or schedule to work on unblocked items; adjust iteration scope with the product owner
Raise a change request The fix needs a baseline or document change (time, money, scope, specification) Move a milestone, add funding, change a requirement (Topic 29)
Escalate Beyond your authority, persistent, or severe and urgent Take it to the sponsor or governance with facts and options (section 10)
Temporary workaround Beyond PMBOK 8 Work must continue while the cause is addressed A manual process, a stub or test double; keep the item open
Add capacity or skills The blocker is a shortage, not an outside dependency Training, mentoring, a short-term specialist
Accept and adjust Impact is low or removal costs more than it returns Document the decision; adjust the plan and expectations
Prevent recurrence The cause is systemic Change the process or working agreement; update OPAs (Topic 31)

Apply it

  1. Match the strategy to the cause and the impact; combine strategies if needed (a workaround now, removal of the cause later).
  2. Assign an owner, an action and a date. The owner must be able to act.
  3. Act within your authority; use influence and negotiation beyond it; escalate what you cannot decide (section 10).
  4. Tell the team and the affected stakeholders what is being done and when to expect relief.
  5. Track progress in the log and verify the effect (section 7).

Leader behavior. PMBOK 8 lists support among the servant-leader behaviors: helping team members through problem-solving and removing impediments builds a supportive culture and a trusting, collaborative environment (Topic 25). The project manager or scrum master:

  • removes the impediments the team cannot (outside groups, approvals, access, policy);
  • shields the team from interruptions and unplanned requests: they go through the product owner and the backlog (Topic 29);
  • lets the team solve what is within its reach instead of solving everything personally;
  • does not just record a recurring delay, ask the team to plan around it permanently, or assign blame.

Pitfalls: logging without acting · adding capacity as the first move · repeating the same fix · stopping all work · waiting for someone else to notice.

7Reassess Continually (ECO)

  • Impediments move. A blocker can be cleared on paper and still slow the team, shift into a new form, or be re-created by the fix.
  • Ask the team. Check from the team's perspective whether the blocker is gone or has shifted. Confirming that your arrangement was made is not the same as confirming that work flows.
  • Mechanisms: the daily coordination meeting (PMBOK 8 lists obstacle identification among its purposes) · retrospectives (at least once per iteration, with specific actions and owners; Topic 31) · regular status and impediment-list reviews · follow-up with the owners of actions.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8 Watch the trend: number of open items, how long each has been open, repeat blockers and time lost to waiting.
  • Repeats are a signal. If the same impediment keeps returning, or several teams report the same one, treat it as systemic: analyze the root cause together (for example in a cross-team retrospective), assign an owner, and change the process or update the OPAs (Topic 31).
  • Close only when work flows. Record the date, the result and what was learned.
  • Stale items: if nothing moves, raise the visibility and escalate.

8Recognize When a Risk Becomes an Issue (ECO)

(See the diagram in section 2.)

How you notice: a stated event has happened (an authority announces a delay, a supplier fails, a test fails, a key person leaves) · a risk trigger in the register has fired · Monitor Risks (tracking identified risks, finding new ones, checking that responses work) or status data show it · the team reports it.

What to do

  1. Confirm the facts.
  2. Log it in the issue log with an owner, an action and a date.
  3. Implement the planned response (the response and reserves defined in the plan; Implement Risk Responses). If the response needs more than the contingency reserve, follow the governance route for more funding (Topics 17 and 21).
  4. Update the risk register and the risk report: record that the risk occurred, what happened and its status. Do not simply raise the probability to 100%, and do not add a duplicate risk for the same event.
  5. Check the knock-on effects: secondary and residual risks, new risks, effects on schedule, cost, scope, quality and benefits; raise a change request if a baseline or document must change (Topic 29).
  6. Inform stakeholders (communications plan), escalate what is beyond your authority and capture the lesson.

Related situations

  • No response was planned (an unforeseen event): it arrives as an issue. Evaluate the impact, collaborate on a resolution, act (a workaround may be needed, Beyond PMBOK 8), then update the register for any new risks it reveals.
  • A risk that never occurs, or whose window has passed, is closed in the register; it does not become an issue.
  • Keep the register alive. A register last updated at kickoff is stale: set a regular review cadence and update statuses (occurred, expired, new) at each review, instead of archiving it, replacing it once or starting again.
  • Escalated risks: once a valid escalation is accepted, ownership moves and the project team no longer monitors the risk (Topic 21).
  • Read the logs together. PMBOK 8 notes that reviewing the issue log and the risk register can reveal challenges tied to individual stakeholders, and the stakeholder domain uses both, with the stakeholder register, to check whether risk responses were implemented successfully.

9Collaborate with Stakeholders to Resolve Issues (ECO)

  • Identify the right people: who is affected, who owns the cause, who has the authority, who can help (stakeholder register; Topic 13).
  • Bring them together when several stakeholders are affected, above all when each proposes a different fix. Agree one approach with them. Do not simply adopt the proposal of the most affected party, the highest-ranking person or the owner of the cause.
  • Use a structured approach: define the problem and its impact together; find the root cause; generate options; evaluate them against agreed criteria (cost-benefit or multicriteria decision analysis); decide; implement; verify.
  • Use facilitation, negotiation and conflict management to keep the discussion on the problem and on project objectives (Topic 26). PMBOK 8 describes facilitation as helping a team build consensus, resolve conflicts and make decisions.
  • Decide at the right level: the team decides within its authority; decisions beyond it are escalated with alternatives and their impacts.
  • Record decisions, owners and dates in the issue log and communicate the status and expected relief to the affected stakeholders.
  • External parties: act within the agreement (service levels, remedies, dispute steps), escalate through the other party's management, and send contract changes through change control (Topics 22 and 29).
  • Where the resolution changes a baseline, raise a change request (Topic 29).
  • Be transparent and honest in reporting the issue and its effects (Topic 06).

10Escalation: When, How and To Whom

What PMBOK 8 says

  • Escalation is a governance component in predictive environments: it helps where decision authority sits outside the team, or where higher-ranking people can remove persistent obstacles or resolve conflicts (Topic 12).
  • The communications management plan holds the project's escalation processes; governance tracks risks together with their escalation criteria.
  • Lead the Team includes resolving and escalating issues.
  • The sponsor, customer and product owner provide decision leadership beyond the project management team's authority, including addressing issues or removing obstacles the team cannot (Standard §2.5.2).
  • For decisions beyond the team's authority, the team investigates alternatives, considers the impact of each and escalates to the person with the proper authority: "do not bring me problems, bring me solutions."

Escalate when

  • the decision, money, resource or policy is beyond your authority;
  • the cause sits outside the project (another department, a vendor's management);
  • it persists after reasonable attempts, or its impact is severe and time-critical;
  • a compliance, safety or ethical threat is involved;
  • an unresolved conflict is disrupting the work (Topic 26).

How to escalate

  • Use the defined path and thresholds (governance framework, communications management plan).
  • Bring the facts and impact, what was tried, the options with their impacts, your recommendation, the decision needed and by when.
  • Agree who owns the matter after the hand-off, and keep working the parts you can.
  • If no path or threshold exists, work with the sponsor to define it. Do not guess it from past decisions or split an order to get under a limit.

Do not: escalate before analysis or reasonable attempts · skip levels without cause · escalate without facts and options · hide a blocked item from the sponsor · escalate and then walk away.

After you escalate: a risk accepted by the receiving party is no longer monitored by the project team. Beyond PMBOK 8practice An escalated issue stays in the issue log until work flows again; ask for a decision date and follow up.

11The Issue Log and Impediment List

Artifact What it is Where it fits
Issue log Project document where issues are recorded and monitored An output of Manage Project Execution; used in Monitor and Control Project Performance, Lead the Team, Monitor Risks and other processes; an input to Close Project or Phase
Impediment list Visual chart: description, severity, actions being taken Team board or information radiator (a visual control)
Change log Record of change requests and decisions Tracks resolutions that alter baselines (Topic 29)
Risk register and risk report Where occurred risks are updated Linked to the issue log by ID Beyond PMBOK 8practice
Lessons learned register Lessons from resolved issues Topic 31

Typical content of an issue log entry [Beyond PMBOK 8 — practice]: ID · description · date raised and by whom · affected work or objective · impact and severity · priority · owner · strategy and actions · due date · status (open, in progress, escalated, resolved, closed) · resolution and date · links to the related risk or change request · lessons.

Use and care

  • Keep one current version, accessible to those who need it (Topic 28).
  • Show open issues, their age, the top impediments and the help needed in status reports.
  • At closure, Close Project or Phase expects documents and deliverables updated and all issues resolved. Anything still open needs a formal decision and a named owner before the project closes (Topic 35).

12Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Where items are captured Issue log; status meetings; reviews Daily coordination meeting; impediment list on the board; retrospectives Both
Who removes them Project manager with the item's owner; escalation to the sponsor or governance The team removes what it can; the scrum master or project manager removes the rest; sponsor, product owner and management beyond Both
Priority driven by Effect on baselines, critical path and risk Effect on the iteration goal, flow and value Baseline envelope first; flow inside it
Cadence Periodic review (for example weekly status) Daily; retrospective each iteration Mixed
Escalation Defined path and thresholds; governance board To the scrum master or project manager, then the sponsor; guardrails set the team's own authority Formal thresholds for the envelope
Risk to issue Risk register to issue log; planned response run Risks visible in the backlog; once occurred, an issue, impediment or backlog item Both
Change Change request when a baseline moves Backlog item and product owner decision Mixed

13Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor the formality of logs, thresholds and reviews to size, complexity, regulation, contract terms and team distribution: a small co-located team may need only a board and a daily meeting; a regulated or contract-driven project needs formal logs and defined escalation paths; distributed teams need shared electronic tools.
  • Interactions: risk (risk to issue), scope and backlog (reordering), schedule (re-sequencing, critical path), finance (reserves), resources (capacity and skills), stakeholders (collaboration, expectations), communications (escalation processes), governance (authority and thresholds), procurement (vendor issues), quality (defects), compliance (nonconformances) and change control.
  • Check results. PMBOK 8's stakeholder-domain check for risk responses is to review the issue log, risk register and stakeholder register. Beyond PMBOK 8practice Healthy signs: fewer open issues and shorter aging, fewer repeat blockers, less time lost to waiting, and stakeholders who know the status of the items that affect them.

14Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. A recurring impediment needs action, not another log entry. Work with the owning group; removing outside blockers is the servant leader's job.
  2. Prioritize by impact and work the highest first. Do not spread the team across every item or work in arrival order.
  3. Do not repeat a failed fix. Evaluate the impact and choose a different strategy (work around, replace, reprioritize); do not stop all work.
  4. Reassess with the team. Ask whether the blocker is cleared or has shifted; do not only verify your own arrangement or add capacity.
  5. A risk that has occurred is an issue. Log it, run the planned response, update the register. Do not raise the probability to 100% or add a duplicate risk.
  6. An unforeseen event is an issue, not a risk: evaluate, collaborate, act, then update the register with what it reveals.
  7. Every item gets one owner, an action and a date.
  8. Beyond your authority: escalate with facts and options. If no path exists, define it with the sponsor. Do not escalate first, skip analysis, split orders or hide it.
  9. Collaborate: bring the affected stakeholders together to agree one approach; do not pick the loudest, the highest-ranking or the most affected.
  10. Fix the root cause. Repeats and shared problems are systemic: cross-team analysis and an update to the process or OPAs.
  11. Change requests resolve issues that move a baseline; never change a baseline informally (Topic 29).
  12. Make impediments visible: impediment list or board, daily meeting, honest status reports.
  13. Keep the registers current by a regular cadence; one refresh at kickoff is not enough.
  14. Be honest: do not soften or delay bad news (Topic 06).
  15. Closing: all issues resolved, or formally handed over with an owner, before the project closes.

15Exam Q&A

15.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Which statement describes a risk, rather than an issue?

  • AThe certification lab has announced a three-week delay to its review
  • BThe sponsor has asked to move the launch date one month earlier
  • CThe test environment is down, and the team cannot proceed with testing
  • DThe certification lab might not finish its review before the launch date
Show the answer

Answer: D. A risk is an uncertain future event that has not yet occurred, signaled by words such as might or could. A delay already announced is an issue, a blocked team faces an impediment, and a request to change a date is a change request.

S2The agile team's impediment list gives only a description of each blocker, and leadership cannot tell how serious each one is or what is being done. What should be added?

  • AThe root cause of each impediment, recorded only after it has been removed
  • BThe names of the team members who first reported each impediment
  • CA weekly summary of the hours lost to each impediment since the project began
  • DThe severity of each impediment and the actions being taken to resolve it
Show the answer

Answer: D. An impediment list is a visual control showing each impediment's description, severity and the actions being taken, kept where the team and stakeholders look. Reporter names, backward-looking summaries or after-the-fact causes do not show urgency or progress.

S3A flaky test environment keeps blocking the scrum team, so it uses a stub to keep working, and the project manager proposes closing the impediment. What is the better approach?

  • AClose it, because work is now flowing and the team is no longer blocked
  • BClose it and move the matter to the lessons learned register instead
  • CKeep it open until the real fix, since the stub works around the cause
  • DClose it and record the stub as a permanent solution for future teams
Show the answer

Answer: C. A workaround keeps work moving while the cause remains, so the item stays open until the real fix. Closing it, calling the stub permanent or moving it to lessons learned leaves the cause unresolved.

S4A flood that nobody anticipated closes the only access road to the site, and no response was planned. What is the best approach?

  • AWait for the water to drop before taking any action on the project itself
  • BAsk the sponsor to cancel the affected work packages for the project
  • CLog it as a risk with a high probability and review it next month
  • DEvaluate the impact, work out a resolution, then update the risk register
Show the answer

Answer: D. An unforeseen event arrives as an issue: the project manager evaluates the impact, works with stakeholders on a resolution (possibly a workaround) and then updates the register for any new risks it reveals. Waiting, logging it as a future risk or canceling work are not responses.

S5The risk register includes a storm-season risk, and the season ended without incident. What should the project manager do with the risk?

  • ARaise its probability to 100% to show that the exposure was real
  • BKeep monitoring it until the end of the project in case the storms return
  • CClose it in the register, since its window has passed and it did not occur
  • DConvert it into an issue, because the project was exposed to the storms
Show the answer

Answer: C. A risk that never occurs, or whose window has passed, is closed in the register and does not become an issue. Converting it, monitoring indefinitely or rescoring it keeps a dead risk alive and distorts exposure.

S6The project manager escalated a stalled approval to the sponsor two weeks ago, and nothing has happened since. What should the project manager do?

  • AFollow up for a decision date and keep the issue logged
  • BClose the issue in the log, since it now belongs to someone else
  • CEscalate the same matter to the sponsor's manager without informing the sponsor
  • DAssume the sponsor is handling it and wait for news about the approval
Show the answer

Answer: A. After escalating, the project manager asks for a decision date, keeps working what can be done and leaves the issue in the log until work flows again; escalating and walking away is a pitfall. Assuming, skipping a level or closing the item loses control.

S7A team member wants to escalate a delayed approval to the sponsor after only one day of waiting, before contacting the approver. What should the project manager advise?

  • AWait silently until the delay has reached a month before saying anything
  • BAsk the team member to hide the delay to avoid bothering the sponsor
  • CContact the approver first, then escalate with facts if it persists
  • DEscalate at once, because senior leaders should know about every delay
Show the answer

Answer: C. Escalation follows reasonable attempts and analysis, and uses facts, impact, options and a recommendation rather than being the first move. Escalating at once, waiting a month or hiding the delay misuses the path.

S8Testers on an agile team report that they cannot proceed, and the project manager's first reaction is to ask the sponsor for extra funding for contractors. What should have come first?

  • AEvaluate the impact and cause before choosing an intervention
  • BHiring the contractors immediately to be sure that testing is covered
  • CAsking the testers to work overtime until the blocker disappears
  • DStopping all other project work until the testers' situation is clear
Show the answer

Answer: A. Understanding comes before action: what is blocked, for whom and for how long, and the cause, shape the intervention strategy. Adding capacity as the first move, stopping all work or overtime treats the symptom.

S9The team's nightly builds fail every Monday, and each time the team restarts the server and goes back to the sprint's stories. What should the project manager encourage?

  • AWaiting to see whether the failures stop by themselves over time
  • BRoot cause analysis to find why it recurs, and a fix that prevents it
  • CDocumenting the restart procedure so that the restart is faster each Monday
  • DAsking the team to start the server earlier on Mondays
Show the answer

Answer: B. A recurring failure handled by the same temporary fix points to an unresolved root cause, so the team finds why it happens and prevents it. Streamlining the restart, shifting its timing or waiting keeps the workaround in place.

S10Reviewing the issue log and the risk register together, the project manager sees that five issues and three risks all involve the same department's approvals. What does this suggest?

  • ANormal noise in the logs, since unrelated entries often look alike
  • BA challenge tied to one stakeholder group, to be addressed through engagement
  • CA reason to merge the two logs so that duplicates disappear
  • DA reason to reassign all the entries to the project manager
Show the answer

Answer: B. Reading the issue log and the risk register together can reveal challenges tied to individual stakeholders or groups, which are then handled through engagement and resolution. Dismissing the pattern, merging the logs or taking over the entries misses the signal.

15.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is an impediment?

Show the answer

An obstacle that prevents the team from achieving its objectives; also called a blocker.

R2How does an issue differ from a risk?

Show the answer

An issue is a current condition that has occurred or is occurring and may need immediate action; a risk is an uncertain possible future event.

R3Where are issues recorded, and what does an impediment list show?

Show the answer

Issues are recorded and monitored in the issue log. An impediment list shows each impediment's description, severity and the actions being taken.

R4In what order do you tackle several open impediments?

Show the answer

By impact (and urgency), highest first, each with one owner, instead of spreading effort across all of them.

R5What do you do before choosing a fix for an impediment?

Show the answer

Evaluate its impact and find the root cause.

R6What are PMBOK 8's problem-solving steps?

Show the answer

Define the problem, identify the root cause, generate possible solutions, choose the best one, implement it and verify that it worked.

R7What should the project manager do about a blocker the team raises every day?

Show the answer

Act: work with the owning group or escalate to remove or reduce it. Recording it again is not management.

R8How do you confirm that an impediment is really resolved?

Show the answer

Ask the team, from its own perspective, whether it is cleared or has shifted, and confirm that work flows again.

R9What do you do when a risk occurs?

Show the answer

Treat it as an issue: log it, implement the planned response, update the risk register and report, check the knock-on effects, inform stakeholders and escalate what is beyond your authority.

R10What is a risk trigger?

Show the answer

An event or condition that indicates a risk is about to occur; it is recorded in the risk register.

R11When should an issue be escalated?

Show the answer

When it is beyond your authority, the cause lies outside the project, it persists after reasonable attempts, it is severe and urgent, or it involves a compliance, safety or ethical threat.

R12What should an escalation contain?

Show the answer

The facts and impact, what was tried, the alternatives with their impacts, a recommendation, and the decision needed and by when.

Topic Key fact
ECO task Remove impediments and manage issues (Business Environment Task 4)
Impediment Obstacle that blocks the team's objectives (blocker); an issue seen from the team's work
Issue Current condition that has occurred or is occurring; a risk is a possible future event
Records Issue log (recorded and monitored); impediment list (description, severity, actions)
Loop Capture, evaluate impact, prioritize and highlight, intervene, reassess, close and learn
Evaluate What, who, how long, effect on objectives; find the root cause (define, root cause, options, choose, implement, verify)
Prioritize By impact and urgency; highest first; one owner each
Highlight Visible impediment list or board; first item at the daily meeting; report to sponsor and governance
Interventions Remove the cause · work with the owning group · negotiate · re-plan · change request · escalate · temporary workaround
Reassess Ask the team: cleared or shifted? Repeats and shared problems are systemic
Risk to issue Confirm, log, planned response, update the register (not "100%"), check effects, inform, learn
Collaborate Bring affected stakeholders together; structured problem-solving; decide at the right level
Escalate Beyond authority, outside the project, persistent, severe or compliance; bring facts and options; define a missing path with the sponsor
Agile angle Team removes what it can; scrum master or project manager removes the rest and shields the team
Closure All issues resolved before Close Project or Phase
